pos: n. (the office and government of the bishop of Rome; the system built upon it)
etymology: Late Latin papatia, from papa, father — a title given to any bishop in the early centuries and claimed exclusively by Rome from the sixth.
biblical_def: The papacy is the claim that one bishop is the visible head of the whole church on earth, Christ's vicar, with universal jurisdiction and, since 1870, an infallible voice. Scripture gives the church one Head (Eph 1:22–23), one Mediator — “there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — and forbids the title the office rests on: “call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven” (Mat 23:9). Peter, of whom the claim is made, wrote to elders as a fellow elder, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3), and the Lord had already refused the pattern: “the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them… but it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:25–26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines papacy as the office and dignity of the pope, or bishop of Rome; popedom.
webster_full: PAPACY, n. The office and dignity of the pope or bishop of Rome; popedom.
2. Papal authority.
scriptures: Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
Eph 1:22
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
corruption_summary: The headship of the church is given to a man, and Scripture gives the church one Head and calls another claimant the man of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The Second London Confession says of the church that the Lord Jesus Christ is the only Head thereof, and that the pope of Rome cannot in any sense be head, but is that antichrist, that man of sin, and son of perdition, that exalteth himself in the church against Christ. That is strong language, and it is Paul's: “Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God” (2Th 2:4). The Reformers did not reach that identification out of national feeling; they reached it because the marks matched — a man seated in the temple, not against the church from outside but within it, claiming what belongs to Christ alone.

The exegetical case for the office rests on one verse, Matthew 16:18, and on a chain of inferences the verse does not carry: that the rock is Peter rather than his confession, that Peter's primacy was transferable, that it was transferred to Rome, and that it descends unbroken. Every link is asserted rather than shown. Peter himself supplies the counter-testimony twice — he calls himself an elder among elders and forbids lordship over the flock — and in Acts 15 it is James who sums up the council, and in Galatians 2 it is Peter who is withstood to the face because he was to be blamed.

The modern temptation is the opposite error: to treat the whole question as a sixteenth-century quarrel that charity should now let drop. But the doctrine at stake is not organisational. If one man holds the keys, dispenses the merit of the saints, and speaks infallibly, then the sufficiency of Christ's priesthood, the sufficiency of Scripture, and justification by faith alone all fall together; and if he does not, the office is a usurpation however gently it is exercised. Charity may soften the tone of the argument. It cannot settle it.
roots_summary: Greek kephale (G2776), head, used of Christ over the church; papas, father, the title of Matthew 23:9; episkopos (G1985), overseer, the office Scripture does give.
roots_lines: Greek kephale (G2776) — head; Ephesians 1:22, 4:15, 5:23, Colossians 1:18, the church's one Head.
Greek pater (G3962) — father; Matthew 23:9, the title forbidden as a religious style.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2 — always plural in a single city.
usage: “Call no man your father upon the earth” — the title the office is built on.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” — Peter on the pattern of oversight.
“He as God sitteth in the temple of God” — the mark the Confession applied.

pos: n. (a high priest; in Roman usage, the pope, styled pontifex maximus)
etymology: Latin pontifex, literally bridge-builder, the title of the chief priest of pagan Rome; taken over by the bishops of Rome after the empire became Christian.
biblical_def: A pontiff is a high priest, and the word carries its own argument: the title pontifex maximus belonged to the chief priest of the Roman state religion before it was assumed by the bishop of Rome. Scripture knows one High Priest under the new covenant — “we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Heb 4:14) — whose priesthood is unchangeable “because he continueth ever” (Heb 7:24), and one bridge between God and men, “the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Every believer is a priest in Him: “ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pontiff as a high priest; and applies the term particularly to the pope, the sovereign pontiff.
webster_full: PONTIFF, n. A high priest. The Jews had one high priest, who officiated in the temple.
2. The pope, so called from his being the chief priest of the Romish church.
scriptures: Heb 4:14
Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
Heb 7:24
But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Heb 7:27
Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
corruption_summary: A standing human priesthood is maintained under the new covenant, and Hebrews argues that the priesthood which continueth ever admits no successor.
corruption_paragraphs: The letter to the Hebrews spends four chapters on a single point: the old priests were many, “because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death” (Heb 7:23), and Christ has an unchangeable priesthood because He continueth ever. A succession is what mortality requires; the whole force of the argument is that His does not require one. To install a standing human pontiff under the new covenant is not to supplement that priesthood but to contradict the reason Hebrews gives for its finality.

The word's history is its own commentary. Pontifex maximus was the office of the emperor as head of Rome's state religion, and the church that took the title also took a good deal of the apparatus — the vestments, the calendar, the altars, the mediating caste. The Reformers' complaint was not aesthetic. A priest is a man who stands between, and where a priest stands between, the veil that was rent from the top to the bottom (Mat 27:51) has been quietly sewn up again. First Peter 2:5 gives the only priesthood the new covenant knows besides Christ's, and it is the whole congregation.
roots_summary: Greek archiereus (G749), high priest; hiereus (G2409), priest; mesites (G3316), mediator; Latin pontifex, bridge-builder, chief priest.
roots_lines: Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest; Hebrews 2:17, 4:14–15, 7:26, 9:11.
Greek hierateuma (G2406) — a priesthood; 1 Peter 2:5, 2:9, of the whole church.
Greek mesites (G3316) — mediator; 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24.
usage: “He continueth ever” — the reason His priesthood admits no successor.
“One mediator between God and men” — the only bridge the word claims to name.
“An holy priesthood” — said of the congregation, not a caste.

pos: n. pl. (adherents of the pope; the Reformation-era name for Roman Catholics)
etymology: From papa, pope, with the suffix of party: those who hold by the pope. A polemical word of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, used throughout the Institutes and the confessions.
biblical_def: Papists is the name the Reformers and the confessions give to those who hold the pope's authority and the doctrines defined at Trent. The word appears constantly in Calvin and in the seventeenth-century divines, and the modern reader meets it in the Institutes and in the older Reformed literature. The dispute it names is stated by the Lord in one sentence: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9), spoken to men who had made the word of God of none effect by their tradition (Mat 15:6). Paul's rule of assurance stands over the same ground: “if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace” (Rom 11:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines papist as a Roman Catholic; one that adheres to the church of Rome and the authority of the pope.
webster_full: PAPIST, n. A Roman catholic; one that adheres to the church of Rome and the authority of the pope.
scriptures: Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Mat 15:6
And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition.
Rom 11:6
And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Mar 7:7
Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: The word is used as a slur or dropped as impolite, and its proper use is to name a doctrinal position, not to despise the people who hold it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite corruptions attend the word. The first is to use it as an insult — a way of dismissing neighbours, colleagues, and often relatives whose sincerity is not in question. The Reformers' quarrel was with a system of doctrine, and the confessions argue against propositions, not against persons; a Protestant who uses the word to feel superior has borrowed the vocabulary of the Reformation without any of its seriousness, since the men who coined it were prepared to be burned over the difference and were not merely being rude.

The second corruption is to retire the word and with it the question. It has become impolite in most quarters to say that a communion which anathematised justification by faith alone at Trent, and has never withdrawn the anathema, teaches another gospel. Galatians 1:8 is the standard the apostle himself set, and he applied it to an angel from heaven. The honest position is neither the sneer nor the silence: to say plainly what is believed on both sides, to acknowledge what is genuinely held in common in the creeds, and to leave the judgment of individual souls where it belongs.
roots_summary: Greek paradosis (G3862), tradition, that which is handed down; entalma (G1778), a commandment of men; euaggelion heteron (G2087, G2098), another gospel.
roots_lines: Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition; Matthew 15:2–6, Mark 7:8–13, Colossians 2:8; and of apostolic teaching, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
Greek entalma (G1778) — a precept of men; Matthew 15:9, Mark 7:7, Colossians 2:22.
Greek anathema (G331) — accursed; Galatians 1:8–9.
usage: “Teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” — the charge the word carries.
“If by grace, then is it no more of works” — the article the dispute turns on.
“Though we, or an angel from heaven” — the standard Paul set for himself first.

pos: n. (the Roman rite of the eucharist, held to be a propitiatory sacrifice)
etymology: Late Latin missa, from the dismissal formula Ite, missa est at the close of the service; the name of the dismissal became the name of the rite.
biblical_def: The mass is the Roman service of the eucharist, defined at Trent as a true and propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest for the living and the dead. Hebrews sets the whole weight of its argument against exactly that: “every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (Heb 10:11), “but this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12), “for by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). He “needeth not daily… to offer up sacrifice… for this he did once, when he offered up himself” (Heb 7:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mass as the service of the Romish church at the celebration of the eucharist; and, as a distinct word, a lump, a body of matter, a great quantity.
webster_full: MASS, n. In the Roman Catholic church, the office or prayers used at the celebration of the eucharist; the consecration of the bread and wine.
MASS, n. A lump; a body of matter concreted, collected or formed into a lump.
2. A large quantity; a collective body.
3. Bulk; magnitude.
scriptures: And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins:
But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Heb 7:27
Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
Heb 9:26
For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
corruption_summary: A sacrifice is offered again, and Hebrews proves the sacrifice finished by the fact that the Priest sat down.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument of Hebrews 10 turns on a posture. Every priest under the law standeth daily, offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins; this Man, having offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. A seated priest is a finished sacrifice, and the writer draws the conclusion himself two verses later: “Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin” (Heb 10:18). A rite that offers again, however reverently, denies in its action the thing it means to honour, and the calendar of its repetition is the confession that it has not finished.

The Reformed objection is not to the Supper's solemnity or to calling it a sacrifice of praise; the Confession itself calls the ordinance a memorial and a spiritual feeding, and treats it with more seriousness than most of its modern heirs. The objection is to propitiation. The Supper shews the Lord's death till he come (1Co 11:26) — it proclaims a death already died, and it does not re-present it to the Father. Rome's own definition at Trent, that the sacrifice of the mass is truly propitiatory and that by it the anger of God is appeased, is the sentence Hebrews was written to make impossible.

There is a Protestant corruption of the same doctrine, which is to make the Supper nothing at all — a monthly formality with no presence, no feeding, and no fear. The Confession's word is that worthy receivers do really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified. Between a sacrifice repeated and a symbol emptied, the Reformed have held a third thing: a real feeding on a finished work.
roots_summary: Greek thusia (G2378), a sacrifice; prosphora (G4376), an offering; hapax (G530) and ephapax (G2178), once, once for all.
roots_lines: Greek thusia (G2378) — sacrifice; Hebrews 10:11–12, 10:26, 13:15, the sacrifice of praise.
Greek prosphora (G4376) — offering; Hebrews 10:10, 10:14, 10:18.
Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10, Romans 6:10.
usage: “This man… sat down on the right hand of God” — a seated priest is a finished sacrifice.
“Where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin” — the writer's own conclusion.
“Ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” — proclaimed, not re-presented.

pos: n. and v. (desert; a claim to reward earned by what one has done)
etymology: Latin meritum, that which is earned, from merere, to deserve. The scholastic vocabulary distinguished merit of condignity from merit of congruity; Scripture uses neither and denies the thing.
biblical_def: Merit is desert — a claim on reward grounded in what the claimant has done. Paul states the arithmetic and then denies its application to sinners: “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:4–5); “if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace” (Rom 11:6). The Lord closes the account for the servant who has kept the whole charge: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). What the believer has is not merit but a gift: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merit as desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honour or reward; worth; and, as a verb, to deserve, to earn by service.
webster_full: MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward; worth; any performance or worth which claims regard or compensation.
2. Value; excellence; applied to things.
MERIT, v.t. To deserve; to earn by active service, or by any valuable performance; to have a right to claim reward in money, regard, friendship or happiness.
scriptures: Rom 4:4
Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Rom 11:6
And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
corruption_summary: Grace is made a help toward earning, and Romans 11:6 says that the moment it is of works it is no more grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 11:6 is the sentence that will not permit a mixture. If by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. Paul does not say the proportion may be adjusted; he says the two are of different kinds, and that admitting works into the ground of standing destroys the character of the grace, not merely its quantity. Every system that makes grace an assistance toward a merit finally earned — the infused righteousness of Trent, the condign merit of the schoolmen, the modern religion of the decent effort — has been answered before it was framed.

The scholastic distinction is worth knowing because it survives in ordinary speech. Merit of condignity was a strict desert, a genuine claim in justice; merit of congruity was a fitness, whereby God is pleased to reward what He is not obliged to reward. The second sounds humble and is the more dangerous, because it concedes the word while keeping the posture: the man still stands before God with something in his hand. Luke 17:10 removes the hand. The servant who has done everything commanded is instructed to call himself unprofitable, which means that perfect obedience would generate no surplus, since duty was owed from the start.

The corollary is the one the Reformed have always insisted on, and it is not licence. If merit is impossible, then works are freed to be what Scripture actually makes them — the fruit and evidence of a life given, not the price of it. Titus 3:5 states both halves in one verse: not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us; and the next verses go straight on to charge that they which have believed be careful to maintain good works. The man who has stopped earning is the only man free to serve.
roots_summary: Greek misthos (G3408), wages, reward; opheilema (G3783), a debt, what is owed; charis (G5485), grace, favour freely given; achreios (G888), unprofitable.
roots_lines: Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, reward; Romans 4:4, Matthew 5:12, 1 Corinthians 3:8, 3:14.
Greek opheilema (G3783) — a debt; Romans 4:4, and of sins, Matthew 6:12.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; Romans 11:6, Ephesians 2:8, Titus 3:7; achreios (G888), unprofitable; Luke 17:10.
usage: “Not reckoned of grace, but of debt” — the arithmetic Paul grants and then withholds from sinners.
“We are unprofitable servants” — said after doing everything commanded.
“Grace is no more grace” — why the mixture cannot be adjusted.

pos: n. pl. (the scholastic theologians of the medieval universities)
etymology: School + men: the masters of the cathedral and university schools, from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries — Lombard, Aquinas, Scotus, Occam — whose method is called scholasticism.
biblical_def: The schoolmen are the theologians of the medieval schools, and Calvin's Institutes argue with them on nearly every page. Their method was rigorous and their distinctions are still useful; their error, as the Reformers saw it, was to let Aristotle set the questions Scripture had not asked, and to build doctrine on inference where the text was silent. Paul's warning is the standing caution: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8), and to Timothy, “avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they do gender strifes” (2Ti 2:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines schoolman as one versed in the niceties of academical disputation or of school divinity; a writer of scholastic divinity.
webster_full: SCHOOLMAN, n. A man versed in the niceties of academical disputation or of school divinity.
2. A writer of scholastic divinity or philosophy.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
corruption_summary: Scholastic care is dismissed as dead precision, and the men who most despise it usually have no doctrine precise enough to defend.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformers were not anti-intellectual and did not despise the schoolmen wholesale; Calvin quotes Lombard and Bernard with respect and reserves his sharpness for what he thinks is sophistry. The complaint is specific: that a method built for logic was made to govern revelation, so that a distinction skilfully drawn could establish a doctrine Scripture never taught — purgatory, the treasury of merit, transubstantiation defended by substance and accident. Colossians 2:8 does not forbid thinking; it forbids being carried off as spoil by a system whose first principles came from somewhere other than Christ.

The modern corruption runs the other way, and it is now the commoner one. A church that has never learned to define its terms calls the discipline of definition dry, prefers testimony to doctrine, and then finds it has no means of telling a heresy from a hymn. The scholastics' vices are unavailable to men who have not attained their virtues. The Reformed answer was not less precision but better warranted precision — the confessions themselves are scholastic in form, carefully articled and closely worded, and they are that way because the men who wrote them had watched loose language cost lives.
roots_summary: Greek philosophia (G5385), philosophy; kenodoxia and apate (G539), deceit; zetesis (G2214), a questioning, disputation; logomacheo (G3054), to strive about words.
roots_lines: Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy; Colossians 2:8 only, with apate (G539), deceit.
Greek zetesis (G2214) — questioning, dispute; 2 Timothy 2:23, 1 Timothy 6:4, Titus 3:9.
Greek logomacheo (G3054) — to strive about words; 2 Timothy 2:14; antithesis (G477), oppositions; 1 Timothy 6:20.
usage: “Spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” — carried off as plunder by a borrowed system.
“Foolish and unlearned questions… gender strifes” — the vice of the method.
“Oppositions of science falsely so called” — Paul's phrase for a learning that misses.

pos: n. pl. (men living under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in a religious house)
etymology: Greek monachos, solitary, from monos, alone; through Latin monachus. The word describes the intended solitude, which the great orders largely gave up for community.
biblical_def: Monks are men bound by vow to poverty, celibacy and obedience within an order. The Reformers judged the institution by two texts. Paul foretells a departing from the faith marked by “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3); and Colossians describes the discipline exactly: things which “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23), in “a voluntary humility” (Col 2:18). The vow itself is not condemned outright — Scripture regulates vows — but a vow to abstain permanently from what God made good is a different thing (1Ti 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines monk as a man who retires from the ordinary temporal concerns of the world, and devotes himself to religion, living in a monastery under vows.
webster_full: MONK, n. A man who retires from the ordinary temporal concerns of the world, and devotes himself to religion.
2. Monks are those who live in monasteries, in obedience to certain rules, and under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience.
scriptures: Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
corruption_summary: Severity toward the body is mistaken for holiness, and Paul says it has a shew of wisdom and no value against the flesh.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:23 is the most exact sentence in Scripture about ascetic religion, and its verdict has two halves. The first is generous: these things have indeed a shew of wisdom — the discipline is impressive, and the man who fasts and watches and sleeps hard genuinely looks holier than the man who does not. The second half is the sting: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. It does not work. Severity toward the body leaves pride untouched and often feeds it, and the sins that destroy monasteries were never the ones the rule was written against.

First Timothy 4 makes the objection doctrinal rather than temperamental. The prohibition of marriage and of meats is named as a mark of the latter times, and the reason given is the goodness of creation: every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. To require permanently of a class of Christians what Paul would not require of any — he honours singleness as a gift and says plainly, if they cannot contain, let them marry — is to turn a gift into a law. The result was foreseeable and is a matter of record.

The Protestant world has no monasteries and has reproduced the error in other forms: the rule that never was commanded, kept as though salvation hung on it, and worn where it can be seen. Every generation finds its own neglecting of the body. The test Paul gives is not whether the discipline is hard but whether it does anything to the flesh, and the honest answer, in the cell or out of it, is usually that it does not.
roots_summary: Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will-worship, self-imposed religion; tapeinophrosune (G5012), humility, here voluntary; apechesthai (G567), to abstain; egkrateuomai (G1467), to contain oneself.
roots_lines: Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — will-worship; Colossians 2:23 only.
Greek koluo gamein (G2967, G1060) — forbidding to marry; 1 Timothy 4:3.
Greek egkrateuomai (G1467) — to contain oneself; 1 Corinthians 7:9, 9:25.
usage: “A shew of wisdom in will worship… not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” — impressive, and ineffective.
“Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” — named as a mark of the latter times.
“Every creature of God is good” — the doctrine the vow contradicts.

pos: n. (the state of being first; the supremacy claimed for the see of Rome)
etymology: Latin primatus, first place, from primus, first. In the controversy the word names Rome's claim to a jurisdiction over all other churches, not merely an honour among them.
biblical_def: Primacy is first place. Scripture assigns it, and not to a see: “he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Col 1:18). Where men sought it among themselves the Lord reversed the order: “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; and whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant” (Mat 20:26–27). John names a man who wanted it in a congregation: “Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not” (3Jn 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines primacy as excellency; the chief place; and, in the church, the chief ecclesiastical station or dignity.
webster_full: PRIMACY, n. Excellency; the chief place.
2. In the church, the chief ecclesiastical station or dignity; the office or dignity of an archbishop.
scriptures: Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.
corruption_summary: First place is sought in the church, and the one word Scripture uses for loving it is spent on Diotrephes.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek noun behind preeminence in Colossians 1:18 and the verb behind Diotrephes's ambition in 3 John 9 are the same root, and the pairing is the whole doctrine. Christ is to have the preeminence in all things; the man who loves to have it among the brethren is named, in the shortest book of the New Testament, as the example of what an elder must not be. Between those two verses there is no room for a third party to hold first place lawfully.

The historical claim is that a primacy of honour among ancient sees became, by degrees, a primacy of jurisdiction over them — a claim the Eastern churches never accepted and the councils of the first centuries did not know. But the argument does not finally rest on history. Matthew 20:26 settles the principle before the history begins: the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion, and it shall not be so among you. Every hierarchy that has grown in the church, Roman or Protestant, has grown against that sentence, and the Reformed insistence on a plurality of elders in each congregation is an attempt to make the sentence structural rather than merely admired.
roots_summary: Greek proteuo (G4409), to be first, have the preeminence; philoproteuo (G5383), to love the first place; diakonos (G1249) and doulos (G1401), minister and servant, the offices Christ substituted.
roots_lines: Greek proteuo (G4409) — to have the preeminence; Colossians 1:18 only.
Greek philoproteuo (G5383) — to love the preeminence; 3 John 1:9 only.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — minister, servant; Matthew 20:26, 23:11, Mark 10:43.
usage: “That in all things he might have the preeminence” — the one lawful primacy.
“Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence” — the same root, in a congregation.
“It shall not be so among you” — the principle stated before the history.

pos: n. pl. (adherents of the church of Rome; a Reformation-era synonym for papists)
etymology: From Rome, with the party suffix. The older Protestant literature uses Romanist, papist and popish almost interchangeably; Rome's own preferred name is Catholic, which the Reformers declined to concede because they claimed catholicity themselves.
biblical_def: Romanists names those who hold the doctrine and authority of the Roman church. The naming itself was part of the argument: the Reformers would not surrender the word catholic, which they confessed every Lord's day in the Creed and understood of the whole body of the elect — “the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” (Heb 12:23) — and so called their opponents by the name of the city rather than by the name of the church universal. Paul had already located catholicity where the Reformers put it: “there is one body, and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:4–5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Romanist as a Roman Catholic; one who adheres to the Romish church.
webster_full: ROMANIST, n. A Roman Catholic; an adherent to the papal church.
scriptures: To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
Eph 4:4
There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;
Eph 4:5
One Lord, one faith, one baptism,

Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:

And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
corruption_summary: Catholicity is conceded to one communion, and the Reformed confess a church universal that no city administers.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary carries a doctrine. When a Protestant says Catholic and means Rome, he has conceded in a word what the Reformation denied in a hundred volumes: that the universal church is a visible institution with an address. The confessions say otherwise. The catholic or universal church, says the Second London Confession, may be called invisible, and consists of the whole number of the elect that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under Christ the head. That church has members in Rome and outside it, and no earthly officer can produce its register.

The corruption in the other direction is sectarian: to treat one's own congregation, denomination, or confession as the whole. The Reformers claimed catholicity precisely because they refused to be a sect — their argument was that they held the faith of the ancient church and the councils, and that Rome had added to it. A man who fights Rome's exclusivity by erecting a smaller one has lost the argument he thinks he is winning, and Hebrews 12:23 is against him too: the assembly is of the firstborn, and their names are written in heaven, which is not a filing system any of us administers.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), the assembly, church; katholikos, universal, whence catholic; Christianos (G5546), Christian, the name given first at Antioch.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — assembly, church; Matthew 16:18, Ephesians 1:22, Hebrews 12:23.
Greek panegyris (G3831) — general assembly; Hebrews 12:23 only.
Greek Christianos (G5546) — Christian; Acts 11:26, 26:28, 1 Peter 4:16.
usage: “The general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” — catholicity with no earthly register.
“One body, and one Spirit… one faith” — where the Reformers located the universal church.
“The disciples were called Christians first in Antioch” — the older name than any party's.

pos: n. (lawful authority to govern and judge, and the extent of it)
etymology: Latin jurisdictio, the speaking of law, from jus, right, and dicere, to say. The word marks not merely power but the bounds within which power is lawful.
biblical_def: Jurisdiction is authority within bounds. The Authorized Version uses the idea at the Lord's trial, where Pilate, hearing that He was a Galilaean, “sent him to Herod” because He “belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction” (Luk 23:7). Scripture assigns distinct spheres: the magistrate bears the sword and is “the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4); the elders rule in the house of God and are told they are not lords over it (1Pe 5:3); and the household has its own government (Eph 6:1–4). Christ's own jurisdiction is without limit: “All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth” (Mat 28:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jurisdiction as the legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; power of executing the laws; and the limit within which power may be exercised.
webster_full: JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
2. Power of governing or legislating.
3. The power or right of exercising authority.
4. The limit within which power may be exercised.
scriptures: Luk 23:7
And as soon as he knew that he belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who himself also was at Jerusalem at that time.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.

And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.
corruption_summary: Church and state each reach into the other's sphere, and Uzziah was struck with leprosy for taking a censer that was not his.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Chronicles 26 is the Old Testament's clearest lesson in jurisdiction, and it happens to a good king. Uzziah, strong and successful, went into the temple to burn incense; eighty priests withstood him — “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests” — and while he raged with the censer in his hand the leprosy rose in his forehead. The offence was not irreligion. He was performing an act of worship, and the sin was that the act was not his to perform. Authority that is real in its own sphere becomes sacrilege the moment it crosses into another's.

The two modern trespasses run in both directions. A state that decides what may be preached, who may gather, and which convictions are lawful has taken the censer; a church that pronounces on questions the magistrate was given the sword to settle, or that tries to govern by political leverage what it has failed to persuade by the Word, has taken the sword. The Reformed have generally held the spheres to be distinct and both under Christ, whose jurisdiction alone is unlimited, and have paid in both currencies when the boundary was violated — sometimes as the victims of a state that overreached, sometimes as the authors of an establishment that did.

Within the church the same principle limits the elder. First Peter 5:3 forbids lordship over God's heritage, and the Confession adds the point that no assembly may bind the conscience beyond what Scripture requires. An elder's jurisdiction is real and it is derived; it extends exactly as far as the Word he is expounding, and where he has no text he has no authority, only an opinion that a congregation may take or leave.
roots_summary: Greek exousia (G1849), authority, right to act; Hebrew mishpat (H4941), judgment, the administration of law; Greek diakrisis, discernment of what belongs where.
roots_lines: Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, jurisdiction; Matthew 28:18, Luke 23:7, Romans 13:1–3, 2 Corinthians 10:8.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, due right; Deuteronomy 1:17, 2 Chronicles 19:6.
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve; Romans 13:4, of the magistrate as God's minister.
usage: “He belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction” — the word at the Lord's trial.
“It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah” — a good king with the wrong censer.
“All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth” — the one unlimited jurisdiction.
